[WP] You are given the chance to become immortal, but the price of this immortality is that upon accepting it you are sent back 3000 years.

It was the year 4907.

The secret to immortality had been discovered, but at a price - when the 'treatment' was administered to someone, they simply disappeared. The tracking devices showed that they were still alive, still in the vicinity of where they had disappeared. No one understood why, or how, but some believed that they existed in another dimension or another time.

I didn't know about that, but all I had to lose was hemophilia B, a very bad case of it. I could bleed out from a simple cut. Besides, I wanted to see what happened when the people disappeared. It was the perfect plan... or so it had seemed.

I had walked into the clinic, chatted idly with the woman behind the counter, and waited. After long hours of paperwork and boredom, I was finally led into a small room and instructed to lie down on a small cot by a robotic voice. A small chip was carefully placed in my head, and then it all went dark.

I awoke in a bed, next to a woman. I blinked in surprise – what had just happened? Where was I?

As I glanced around, I rephrased the mental question. When was I?

The place was wooden, dank and a bit smelly. The woman grumbled in her sleep and stirred slightly. I stood, careful not to disturb her, and quietly left the small dusty house.

I stopped in my tracks outside. What in the world…? If the house had been strange, this village was positively alien.

People milled about, talking and shouting and was that man singing? Well, at least I seemed to fit right in; most of the men had beards as bushy and black as my own.

I was relieved beyond words when I understood their speech. It was somewhat faster and more complicated than my language, but it was mostly similar. I imagined I would sound jumbled and clumsy to them… ah well. What can you do, right? I heard them speaking names, and was doubly relieved to hear that theirs were similar to mine. If this really was the past, perhaps some of this land’s culture had survived in mine.

I made to stride forward, but I was stopped by a man dressed in clothes that would probably be very fancy if they didn’t look so ridiculous. I stifled a chuckle as he began to speak to me. I made out about half the words, but the gist was that someone wanted to see me…

Well, I was immortal. What was the worst that could happen? I went with him, and before I knew it I was standing in a great hall, staring at who could only be a very powerful man. He spoke to me, and I understood that someone he loved was ill. His son, perhaps? His wife?

I was whisked away to a chamber where a young boy lay on a bed. Son, then. He looked terrible, to say the least. His face was pale as death, and he could barely raise his arm. I stepped forward to examine him.

A wound stretched across his stomach, and it bled profusely. I wasn’t entirely sure what to do, until I realized that it was the very same condition that had plagued me prior to my immortalization… or at least I hoped I was immortal now. I would be very peeved if it hadn’t worked and I’d been sent here for nothing.

I knew how to help the boy. I spoke words that I had learned from the healers of my time, touched the wound in the right way, dropped to my knees and stared at him, and the bleeding slowed. It was very subtle, but I caught it, as I had learned to from all the times I had been temporarily healed. The boy would be fine in a few days, until he suffered another injury such as this one. I nodded to the anxious people waiting around. They chattered excitedly as I exited the chamber.

I told the powerful man – the ruler of the land, I later discovered – that his son would survive. He was overjoyed and his stoic demeanour cracked for a moment to let through a beaming smile. I smiled back at him.

—

It was 1916, nine years after my immortalization. I had learned the year as soon as I could. I had discovered the truth of my immortality in a very unpleasant manner – an assassination attempt. I had become influential in the politics of the land, and there were those who resented it. I had been stabbed, by a woman who had seemed perfectly normal, and it was as painful and bloody as it would have been, had I been mortal. I would not have survived if I had been mortal, though, despite the doctors’ help.

I had been invited to the house of a man of power, though not as much power as the country’s ruler. I was offered tea and pastries; of course, I accepted, though I would later regret it. I couldn’t have known that the pastries would be laced with a chemical, a poison perhaps, that caused me great discomfort and was probably intended to kill me. At the time, I thought the pastries simply didn’t agree with me. I couldn’t have known that he would shoot me when I was thoroughly drunk, and then twice again when I staggered outside. I couldn’t have known that he would toss me into the freezing river.

To my credit, though, I managed to push myself into a mass of ice, keeping myself steady until I was strong enough to pull myself out of the river. The ordeal made me completely sure of my immortality; after all, what mortal could survive a bullet to the brain?

It took long months for me to recover enough to even stand, and months after that until I could walk. I was back in prime physical condition after years.

I thought of revenge, of making my attacker pay for his crimes. But… no. No, instead I would just leave. My name would go down in this land’s history, perhaps even leak into others, or even the history books of the 4000s. No one would know how I lived through poison and three fatal bullet wounds, only to drown in a burlap sack.

Yes, everyone would remember the name of Rasputin.

EDIT: OPTIONAL ENDING TO TACK ON

It was 2014, and I was powerful.

It had been nearly a century since my supposed ‘death’. I had watched the land change, once again gained political strength. I had changed my face, shaved my beard, and made modifications to my body so there would be no chance of comparison. I had changed my name, but only a bit, just to leave a little hint. No one would make the connection anyway, so there wasn’t any harm.

I wanted my country to grow, to be stronger and better and bigger. I needed land, land that would be easily assimilated into Russia.

I needed Crimea.

So there was this strange noise at first. Birds. I couldn't tell which ones. To me, that was uncommon and made me feel uncomfortable. I know birds.

Then came the arrows. At first, only a few ones flew by me. Their sound also speaking in an uncommon tounge.

When I awoke a man wearing what could be described as a dead bear on top of his head sat in front of me. He moved his hands mysteriously and chanted something. It felt soothing and I tried to focus on the repetative sound of his vowels while I searched the room with my eyes. It was dark but a few fires lit up the surroundings. There were people everywhere. Some holding sticks, others holding small babies. Very few wearing clothes. I felt like I was going to vomit so that is what I did. No one said anything afterwards and the man continued to say whatever he was telling me.

I tried to get up and to my own suprise, I was able to do it without any trouble. The man stopped his chanting and locked his eyes onto me.

"You shouldn't leave", he said. "We're like you. The outside does not like us. We don't belong. That means you will not belong anywhere else but here!"

"You took the deal as well?"

"We all did. We're just here awaiting our time."

I sat down. "That will be a long wait", I said nodding to those who stood around us.

"Yeah! No need to keep track of date nor time. We'll figure out where we are in history as soon as the Europeans come."

At that time, the choice didn't seem too hard. Three thousand years, for a lifespan eternal. I would be there, a diamond pristine and glimmering, never blemished by wind nor rain. I would have forever, to do as I wish, as fleeting mortal lives withered around me.

My first thousand years were spent in wanderings. I walked on foot always, ploughing through jungles, the very bottom of my legs in fresh sea foam as I lined the coasts. It got boring fast, and soon I desired to travel to the New World. My skills as a mechanic were limited, but still I crafted a ship. The wind was swift and blew me quickly across the glistening seas. I would stare into the setting sun, and think of the life I had forsaken. Tears would often creep into my eyes, but always the ghost of a smile would remain across my face. I did not regret what I had done, for I knew that we would be reunited in a thousand more years. It was a simple time then, for I was free to revel alone in the strange beauty of this ancient world.

The next thousand years were heartwrenching. Sightings of the species I now despise grew more and more frequent, and contact soon became unavoidable. I built a modest mud house in Egypt, and there married my first wife. We had three children, and it was with regret that I conceived them, for I knew that I would long outlive them. The ethereal beauty of her youth faded, while I remained young and passionate and she looked upon me with eyes of wonder. I was a son of Ra, she whispered. It was a great blessing, she told me. I had great power, power to bring forth the blazing sun. But it felt like more of a curse.

Her hair slowly greyed, and the once loving look in her eyes had descended into madness and jealously. I did not begrudge her. We quarreled often and so I set off one tender night in search of a life like the one I had led for the past thousand. I think of her frequently still, of her high cheekbones and glossy black hair. In my mind, she is as immortal as me.

After my third failed marriage; the third heart I had broken; the third soul of which fires I had extinguished, I decided that I had learned my lesson. I went as far back to nature as I could, and lived in a stone tower in the jungles of the Amazon for the next five centuries, with only the poison dart frogs and the tigers for company. The natives must have known of my existence, but they did not interrupt my musings, and I was glad for that.

The Industrial Age came, and with it, the greed of Man. Parties of European hopefuls invaded the jungles, with the hope of striking gold amongst its lush vegetation. I stowed away in a ship and headed back to Europe, and I sat out the two great wars in Switzerland, safe and high in the Alps. During this time, I studied the classics and painted and composed, in a desperate and ultimately futile attempt to discern the meaning of my life.

Fast forward. I stormed into the laboratory just after I had been teleported into the past, furious and demanding a cure. I would have welcomed most of all the sweet relief of death. But of course, there were none to be offered, and I spent the night weeping there, the expensive equipment lying in shattered fragments among my broken soul. I had ensured that none would ever follow in my footsteps.

Soon, Man had gone forever and I was the last pitiful echo of their dynasty. I watched as the sun exploded into a blazing supernova, and continued to watch as the universe imploded around me. I became the lone consciousness in a forever of nothing. But without a purpose, the light of my soul began to dim, until it was almost nothing. An eternity later, I began to merge with the nothingness around me. As the last particles of my being fused, I could have sworn I heard a last soft sigh from above. It was reminiscent of the last soft breezes of a dying spring, those that had echoed so sweetly in caves an eternity ago.

And after spring, I knew, was summer.

And so I brought forth the blazing sun. Spring had ended, and now summer would begin.
